title: Lacrosse: overview
d: Lacrosse is a team stick sport played 10 per side (men's field).
definition: Lacrosse is a team stick sport played 10 per side (men's field).
description: Lacrosse is a team stick sport. score more goals than the opponent. The contest is played 10 per side (men's field), and the side that 1 point per goal; most goals wins; overtime settles ties wins. Indigenous North American origins; modern field game codified in 1860s Canada. The sport is governed by official laws that cover the field of play, equipment, players, officials, scoring, fouls, and conduct; this database walks through every one of those areas so a newcomer can follow a full match with understanding.

title: The objective
d: The objective of Lacrosse is: score more goals than the opponent.
definition: The objective of Lacrosse is: score more goals than the opponent.
description: Every rule in Lacrosse exists to serve one objective: score more goals than the opponent. All tactics, positions, and scoring flow from that single aim. Beginners should fix the objective in mind first, because every foul, stoppage, and strategy in the sport is judged against whether it fairly advances or unfairly blocks that objective. Coaches return to it constantly: if a play does not serve the objective, it is the wrong play.

facts.objective: score more goals than the opponent

title: Scoring system
d: In Lacrosse, scoring works as follows: 1 point per goal; most goals wins; overtime settles ties.
definition: In Lacrosse, scoring works as follows: 1 point per goal; most goals wins; overtime settles ties.
description: Scoring in Lacrosse: 1 point per goal; most goals wins; overtime settles ties. Knowing exactly what counts, and how much, changes how you watch: every attack is shaped by the scoring system, and comebacks are measured against it. Scorekeepers record each score the moment it happens, and at most levels the scoreboard is the official record unless a protest is filed under the competition rules.

facts.scoring: 1 point per goal; most goals wins; overtime settles ties

title: How games are won
d: Lacrosse: 1 point per goal; most goals wins; overtime settles ties.
definition: Lacrosse: 1 point per goal; most goals wins; overtime settles ties.
description: Winning Lacrosse comes down to the scoreboard: 1 point per goal; most goals wins; overtime settles ties. Because of that, late-game strategy everywhere in the sport is clock-and-score management — protecting a lead or chasing one changes every decision, from how much risk to take to when to slow play down or speed it up. Champions are often simply the teams that manage the winning condition best in the final minutes.

title: Ties and tiebreakers
d: Tied games in Lacrosse are resolved under the competition rules for the level of play.
definition: Tied games in Lacrosse are resolved under the competition rules for the level of play.
description: Not every contest in Lacrosse can end tied: league games may allow draws while knockout games must produce a winner through extra time, tiebreak procedures, or shootouts defined by the competition. Tiebreak rules are announced before play and never invented mid-game; players and coaches must know them, because they reshape tactics — a team may play for penalties, or gamble everything to avoid them.

facts.note: tiebreak rules are set by the competition, not improvised

title: Match duration
d: Lacrosse contests last: four 15-minute quarters (pro) or halves (college).
definition: Lacrosse contests last: four 15-minute quarters (pro) or halves (college).
description: A Lacrosse contest runs four 15-minute quarters (pro) or halves (college). Duration shapes fitness demands: athletes train to be sharp in the final stretch, not just the first. Timekeeping is an official duty — the clock, not the players, decides when it ends, and added or extra time exists to compensate for stoppages so the advertised duration is genuinely played.

title: Periods and breaks
d: Play in Lacrosse is divided into periods with breaks as defined for the competition.
definition: Play in Lacrosse is divided into periods with breaks as defined for the competition.
description: The four 15-minute quarters (pro) or halves (college) in Lacrosse give coaches their main lever: adjustments, substitutions, and rest happen in the breaks. Teams plan for three phases — start fast, manage the middle, finish strong — and the side that uses its breaks better often wins the second half. Break length and number are fixed by the rules; exceeding them can draw penalties.

title: The venue
d: Lacrosse is played at: field 110 by 60 yards; goals 6ft by 6ft.
definition: Lacrosse is played at: field 110 by 60 yards; goals 6ft by 6ft.
description: The Lacrosse is part of the sport: field 110 by 60 yards; goals 6ft by 6ft. Dimensions, surfaces, and markings are standardized so records and tactics transfer between venues. Groundskeepers and officials inspect the venue before play; an unfit surface can postpone a contest. Players learn to read their venue — wind, sun, surface speed — because the same game plays differently in different buildings.

title: Field dimensions
d: Regulation dimensions for Lacrosse: field 110 by 60 yards; goals 6ft by 6ft.
definition: Regulation dimensions for Lacrosse: field 110 by 60 yards; goals 6ft by 6ft.
description: Regulation Lacrosse dimensions: field 110 by 60 yards; goals 6ft by 6ft. Lines are part of the field of play and officiated precisely — in or out, over the line or not, decides scores. Youth and amateur versions scale the dimensions down, but the proportions and the meaning of every line stay the same so skills transfer up to the full-size game.

title: Playing surface
d: Lacrosse surfaces must be safe, level, and marked to regulation.
definition: Lacrosse surfaces must be safe, level, and marked to regulation.
description: The playing surface in Lacrosse must be safe, level, and marked to regulation. Surface changes tactics: fast surfaces reward speed and quick passing, slow or soft ones reward power and patience. Footwear and equipment rules usually assume a specific surface, and playing on the wrong one risks both injury and disqualification of the contest.

title: Essential equipment
d: Lacrosse requires: stick with mesh pocket, ball, helmet, gloves, pads.
definition: Lacrosse requires: stick with mesh pocket, ball, helmet, gloves, pads.
description: No one plays Lacrosse without: stick with mesh pocket, ball, helmet, gloves, pads. Equipment is inspected — illegal or unsafe gear is removed before play, and at higher levels every item must meet the governing body's specifications. Beginners should buy for safety and fit first, performance second; the right size matters more than the brand.

facts.equipment: stick with mesh pocket, ball, helmet, gloves, pads

title: The ball
d: The Lacrosse ball is specified by the laws: size, weight, and pressure are regulated.
definition: The Lacrosse ball is specified by the laws: size, weight, and pressure are regulated.
description: Where Lacrosse uses a ball, its size, weight, bounce, and pressure are fixed by the laws: stick with mesh pocket, ball, helmet, gloves, pads. Ball specs change the whole game — a lighter, livelier ball rewards touch, a heavier one rewards power. Match balls are approved and often supplied by the competition; warming up with the wrong spec builds the wrong feel.

facts.equipment: stick with mesh pocket, ball, helmet, gloves, pads

title: Protective gear
d: Protection in Lacrosse: required and recommended gear keeps players safe within the laws.
definition: Protection in Lacrosse: required and recommended gear keeps players safe within the laws.
description: Protection is part of the laws of Lacrosse, not an afterthought. Required and recommended gear exists because the sport's known injury patterns are known: the rules mandate the gear that prevents the common ones. Gear must fit and be worn correctly — loose or missing protection can keep a player off the field, and no contest is worth a preventable injury.

title: Team size
d: Lacrosse is played 10 per side (men's field).
definition: Lacrosse is played 10 per side (men's field).
description: Lacrosse is played 10 per side (men's field). Numbers decide the geometry of the game: more players means more structure and specialization, fewer means more space and versatility. Every player must know the legal team size, because playing short — or with too many — brings penalties, and planned rotations are built around the allowed numbers.

title: Positions and roles
d: Positions in Lacrosse divide the work: each role has a zone, duties, and skills.
definition: Positions in Lacrosse divide the work: each role has a zone, duties, and skills.
description: Positions in Lacrosse exist to divide the 10 per side (men's field) into manageable jobs. Each role has a home zone, primary duties, and a skill profile; great teams are built by fitting people to roles, not roles to people. Beginners should learn one position deeply before roaming — mastery of a role teaches the whole game faster than playing everywhere badly.

title: Substitutions
d: Substitution rules in Lacrosse control how and when players may be replaced.
definition: Substitution rules in Lacrosse control how and when players may be replaced.
description: Substitutions in Lacrosse are a tactical weapon governed by strict procedure: only at stoppages, only through the official, only within the allowed number. Coaches plan substitution windows the way generals plan reserves — fresh legs at the right moment win tight games. Illegal substitution procedure can cost a team a player or a penalty.

title: Officials
d: Lacrosse is officiated by: three officials on field.
definition: Lacrosse is officiated by: three officials on field.
description: Lacrosse is officiated by three officials on field. Officials are neutral arbiters of the laws: their decisions on matters of fact are final during play, and dissent is penalized. Knowing what each official watches helps players stay legal — most fouls are committed in full view of exactly the official assigned to that zone.

title: The referee's role
d: The referee in Lacrosse enforces the laws, keeps time, and manages conduct.
definition: The referee in Lacrosse enforces the laws, keeps time, and manages conduct.
description: The referee's job in Lacrosse is bigger than blowing a whistle: enforcing the laws, keeping time, managing conduct, and protecting player safety — in that order. Players may ask for clarification respectfully; they may not dispute decisions. At every level, the referee's authority begins when they enter the venue and ends when they leave it.

d: The ball must be moved with the crosse; hands may not touch it in play.

Understanding the reason behind the rule — the unfair advantage it prevents — makes it easy to remember and to apply at speed. When in doubt during play, the safe choice is the one this rule describes.

facts.rule: The ball must be moved with the crosse; hands may not touch it in play.

title: Fouls
d: Illegal play in Lacrosse draws fouls under the laws; persistent fouling draws cards or ejections.
definition: Illegal play in Lacrosse draws fouls under the laws; persistent fouling draws cards or ejections.
description: A foul in Lacrosse is illegal play as defined by the laws — not just rough play, but any act the rules forbid. Officials grade fouls by intent, danger, and advantage gained; persistent or cynical fouling draws escalating punishment. Smart players learn the exact line: physical right up to it, never across it.

title: Penalties
d: Fouls in Lacrosse are punished by free plays, spot penalties, or loss of possession per the laws.
definition: Fouls in Lacrosse are punished by free plays, spot penalties, or loss of possession per the laws.
description: Punishment in Lacrosse fits the foul: minor infringements restart play for the other side, serious ones award direct scoring chances or remove the offender. Penalty rules are deliberately severe enough that fouling is never a good trade — the team that stays disciplined keeps eleven (or its equivalent) on the field and wins the close ones.

title: Discipline and conduct
d: Misconduct in Lacrosse — dissent, dangerous play, unsporting behavior — is penalized, up to ejection.
definition: Misconduct in Lacrosse — dissent, dangerous play, unsporting behavior — is penalized, up to ejection.
description: The laws of Lacrosse punish misconduct on a ladder: warnings, cards, sin-bins, ejections, suspensions. Dissent, dangerous play, and unsporting behavior are treated as seriously as technical fouls, because the game depends on respect for officials and opponents. Captains are responsible for their team's conduct and speak to the referee for the side.

title: Basic strategy
d: Lacrosse strategy starts from the objective: score more goals than the opponent.
definition: Lacrosse strategy starts from the objective: score more goals than the opponent.
description: All Lacrosse strategy serves the objective: score more goals than the opponent. The basic game plan is simple — win your individual battles, keep your shape, and take the chances the scoring system rewards most. Beginners win by doing simple things reliably; advanced players win by forcing opponents into mistakes while making none themselves.

facts.objective: score more goals than the opponent

title: Offense
d: Attacking in Lacrosse means creating the scoring chances the rules reward.
definition: Attacking in Lacrosse means creating the scoring chances the rules reward.
description: Attacking Lacrosse is about manufacturing the highest-percentage chances the scoring system allows. Good offense is patient until the opening appears, then ruthless: create space, move the defense, and finish. The best attacks look simple because every player knows the plan two passes ahead.

title: Defense
d: Defending in Lacrosse means denying the objective: score more goals than the opponent.
definition: Defending in Lacrosse means denying the objective: score more goals than the opponent.
description: Defending Lacrosse starts from denying the objective: score more goals than the opponent. Good defense is organized first and aggressive second — shape, communication, and patience, with pressure applied where the opponent is weakest. The great defensive teams all share one trait: every player defends, all the time, without being asked.

facts.objective: score more goals than the opponent

title: Origins
d: Origins of Lacrosse: Indigenous North American origins; modern field game codified in 1860s Canada..
definition: Origins of Lacrosse: Indigenous North American origins; modern field game codified in 1860s Canada..
description: The origins of Lacrosse: Indigenous North American origins; modern field game codified in 1860s Canada.. Like most sports, it began as folk play and was formalized when clubs and schools wrote common rules so strangers could compete fairly. Those first written laws are the ancestor of every rule in this database — the game you watch today is their descendant.

facts.history: Indigenous North American origins; modern field game codified in 1860s Canada.

title: Modern era
d: Modern Lacrosse: professional leagues, world championships, and Olympic or global stages.
definition: Modern Lacrosse: professional leagues, world championships, and Olympic or global stages.
description: Modern Lacrosse grew through professional leagues, world championships, and global competition. Television and professionalism standardized the laws worldwide and turned the best players into full-time athletes. The modern game is faster, stronger, and more tactical than any earlier era — but it is played under the same essential objective the founders wrote down.

title: Variations
d: Lacrosse has official and informal variations with adjusted rules for numbers, space, and level.
definition: Lacrosse has official and informal variations with adjusted rules for numbers, space, and level.
description: Every major sport spawns variations: small-sided, beach, indoor, youth, and disability versions of Lacrosse all adjust numbers, space, and rules while keeping the soul of the game. Variations are where most people actually play — the full eleven-a-side (or equivalent) version is the tip of a much bigger pyramid.

title: Safety
d: Play Lacrosse safely: warm up, wear the required gear, follow the foul laws, and stop for injury.
definition: Play Lacrosse safely: warm up, wear the required gear, follow the foul laws, and stop for injury.
description: Safety in Lacrosse is part of the rules, not separate from them: warm up properly, wear every required piece of gear, respect the foul laws that exist to prevent injury, and stop play for any head injury or suspected serious harm. No game, drill, or tryout is worth playing hurt — the laws protect players who protect themselves.
